steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on explaining graph neural networks with simple surrogate models (Distill n' Explain). Motivate the interpretability problem for GNNs, review post-hoc and GNN-specific explanation methods and their assumptions, introduce DnX and FastDnX, summarize the experimental findings, and close with a list of contributions.

  - extensive experiments: better than prior art, orders of magnitude faster

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) are now the pillars of representation learning on graphs. A typical GNN uses message passing on the input graph to get meaningful node or graph representations for the task at hand. GNNs have been successful in many domains, but their architectural design often makes models that are not very interpretable. This makes it hard to diagnose cases where GNNs are fooled by confounding effects or do not align well with expert knowledge.

A popular strategy to deal with this lack of interpretability is to use post-hoc explanation methods. The idea is to make the model more transparent by highlighting the input or model elements that are especially important for the predictions, which helps users to understand what is happening under the hood.

Recently there has been an outbreak of methods for explaining GNNs. GNN explanations come in different flavors, but they usually are (minimal) substructures of the input graph that strongly influence the prediction we want to explain. A seminal work proposes to learn a soft mask that weighs the graph edges. To find meaningful masks, GNNExplainer maximizes the mutual information between the GNN predictions on the original graph and on the masked one. To avoid optimizing again every time we want to explain a different node, another work proposes using node embeddings to parameterize the masks, i.e., amortizing the inference. But GNNExplainer and PGExplainer both make strong assumptions about our access to the GNN we want to explain. GNNExplainer assumes that we can back-propagate through the GNN. PGExplainer also assumes we can access the hidden activations of the GNN. PGMExplainer relaxes these assumptions by approximating the local behavior of the GNN with a probabilistic graphical model (PGM) over components, which can be used to rank how relevant nodes and edges are. However, getting explanations from PGMExplainer involves learning the structure of a PGM, and this may not scale well.

- Our approach
  - same black-box setting as PGMExplainer, much lower cost via global surrogate
  - DnX: distill simple GNN \Psi (e.g. simple graph convolution) mimicking \Phi; convex program -> node mask on \Psi
  - FastDnX: uses linearity of surrogate
  - only evaluations of \Phi; fixed \Psi explains any node-level prediction
  - theory linking distillation quality and faithfulness
- Experiments: eight benchmarks; often beat GNN-, PG-, PGM-Explainers; much faster; up to 65K\times over GNNExplainer; benchmark limitations
- Contributions: framework; theoretical bounds; extensive experiments

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) are now the pillars of representation learning on graphs. A typical GNN uses message passing on the input graph to get meaningful node or graph representations for the task at hand. GNNs have been successful in many domains, but their architectural design often makes models that are not very interpretable. This makes it hard to diagnose cases where GNNs are fooled by confounding effects or do not align well with expert knowledge.

A popular strategy to deal with this lack of interpretability is to use post-hoc explanation methods. The idea is to make the model more transparent by highlighting the input or model elements that are especially important for the predictions, which helps users to understand what is happening under the hood.

Recently there has been an outbreak of methods for explaining GNNs. GNN explanations come in different flavors, but they usually are (minimal) substructures of the input graph that strongly influence the prediction we want to explain. A seminal work proposes to learn a soft mask that weighs the graph edges. To find meaningful masks, GNNExplainer maximizes the mutual information between the GNN predictions on the original graph and on the masked one. To avoid optimizing again every time we want to explain a different node, another work proposes using node embeddings to parameterize the masks, i.e., amortizing the inference. But GNNExplainer and PGExplainer both make strong assumptions about our access to the GNN we want to explain. GNNExplainer assumes that we can back-propagate through the GNN. PGExplainer also assumes we can access the hidden activations of the GNN. PGMExplainer relaxes these assumptions by approximating the local behavior of the GNN with a probabilistic graphical model (PGM) over components, which can be used to rank how relevant nodes and edges are. However, getting explanations from PGMExplainer involves learning the structure of a PGM, and this may not scale well.

In this work we use the same black-box setting as PGMExplainer, but we cut the computational cost a lot by getting explanations from a global surrogate model. Specifically, we propose Distill n' Explain (DnX). DnX uses knowledge distillation to learn a simple GNN \Psi, e.g. simple graph convolution, which mimics the behavior of the GNN \Phi that we want to explain. Then it solves a simple convex program to find a mask that weighs how much each node influences the output of \Psi. We also propose FastDnX, a variant of DnX that uses the linear nature of our surrogate to make the explanation procedure faster. We only need evaluations of \Phi to learn the surrogate \Psi, and after \Psi is fixed we can use it to explain any node-level prediction. To support the intuition that explaining a surrogate instead of the original GNN makes sense, we give a theoretical result that links the distillation quality to how faithful our explanations are.

We run experiments on eight popular node classification benchmarks, and DnX and FastDnX often do better than GNN-, PG-, and PGM-Explainers. Both DnX and FastDnX are also much faster than the competitors. FastDnX is up to 65K\times faster than GNNExplainer. Lastly, we discuss the limitations of the current benchmarks and show that explainers that can use simple inductive biases can ace them.

Our contributions are the following three:

- 1. a new framework for GNN explanations that treats GNNs as black-box functions and explains a simple surrogate model obtained with knowledge distillation;

- 2. theoretical bounds on the quality of explanations based on these surrogates, which link the error in the distillation procedure to the faithfulness of the explanation;

- 3. extensive experiments, which show that our methods outperform the prior art and run orders of magnitude faster.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) [1,2] have become the pillars of representation learning on graphs. Typical GNNs rely on message passing over input graphs to extract meaningful node/graph representations for the task at hand. Despite the success of GNNs in many domains [3,4,5,6], their architectural design often results in models with limited interpretability. This makes it hard to diagnose scenarios in which GNNs are fooled by confounding effects or align poorly with expert knowledge.

To mitigate this lack of interpretability, a popular strategy is to use post-hoc explanation methods [7,8,9,10,11]. The idea is to increase model transparency by highlighting input/model elements that are particularly important for predictions, helping users understand what is happening under the hood.

There has recently been an outbreak of methods for explaining GNNs [12]. Although GNN explanations come in different flavors [13,14,15,16,17], they usually take the form of (minimal) substructures of the input graph that are highly influential to the prediction we want to explain. The seminal work of [13] proposes learning a soft mask to weigh graph edges; to find meaningful masks, GNNExplainer maximizes the mutual information between the GNN predictions given the original graph and the masked one. To avoid optimizing again whenever we want to explain a different node, [18] propose using node embeddings to parameterize the masks, i.e., amortizing the inference. Nonetheless, GNNExplainer and PGExplainer make strong assumptions about our access to the GNN we are trying to explain: the former assumes we can back-propagate through the GNN, and the latter further assumes access to its hidden activations. [19] relieve these assumptions by approximating the local behavior of the GNN with a probabilistic graphical model (PGM) over components, which can be used to rank the relevance of nodes and edges. However, getting explanations from PGMExplainer involves learning the structure of a PGM, which may not scale well.

In this work, we adopt the same black-box setting as [19] but drastically cut down on computational cost by extracting explanations from a global surrogate model. In particular, we propose Distill n' Explain (DnX). DnX uses knowledge distillation to learn a simple GNN \Psi, e.g. simple graph convolution [20], that mimics the behavior of the GNN \Phi we want to explain. It then solves a simple convex program to find a mask that weighs the influence of each node on the output of \Psi. We also propose FastDnX, a variant of DnX that exploits the linear nature of our surrogate to speed up the explanation procedure. Notably, we only need evaluations of \Phi to learn the surrogate \Psi, and once \Psi is fixed we can use it to explain any node-level prediction. To support the intuition that explaining a surrogate instead of the original GNN is sensible, we provide a theoretical result linking distillation quality to the faithfulness of our explanations.

Experiments on eight popular node classification benchmarks show that DnX and FastDnX often outperform GNN-, PG-, and PGM-Explainers. Both DnX and FastDnX are also much faster than the competitors, with FastDnX achieving a speedup of up to 65K\times over GNNExplainer. Finally, we discuss the limitations of current benchmarks and show that explainers able to leverage simple inductive biases can ace them.

Our contributions are three-fold:

- 1. we propose a new framework for GNN explanations that treats GNNs as black-box functions and relies on explaining a simple surrogate model obtained through knowledge distillation;

- 2. we provide theoretical bounds on the quality of explanations based on these surrogates, linking the error of the distillation procedure to the faithfulness of the explanation;

- 3. we carry out extensive experiments showing that our methods outperform the prior art while running orders of magnitude faster.
